TMP brings forward a furniture package for installation in Summer 2026 that continues work around supporting 'Deep Learning' and creating future-ready learning environments aligned with Troy School District's vision. https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.paragraph: A one-page framework titled 'TSD Guiding Principles for Furniture in Future-Ready Learning Environments' that defines the criteria Troy School District uses when selecting classroom furniture. It groups desired qualities into five themes: furniture that supports movement and motion; that inspires student agency and healthy risk-taking; that is comfortable and fosters belonging; that meets the needs of all students and staff; and that encourages innovative pedagogy. It appears as agenda item 8.E at the March 17, 2026 regular Board of Education meeting.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.page:
What it is
A guiding-principles document adopted by Troy School District (TSD) to steer furniture selection for 'Future-Ready Learning Environments,' presented as agenda item 8.E at the March 17, 2026 regular Board of Education meeting.

The five guiding principles
- Supports movement and motion: moves easily around the room, partners with other pieces for multiple configurations, encourages students to move, lets them find a comfortable proximity to others, and aids efficient transitions.
- Supports and inspires student agency and healthy risk-taking: builds self-awareness, can be used in many (even unexpected) ways, sustains engagement, empowers students to show their work, and supports organization and access to tools.
- Comfortable and fosters belonging: gives a feeling of safety, is comfortable to most, lets students organize the space purposefully, feels exciting and joyful, and supports a variety of postures.
- Meets the needs of all students and staff: promotes community ('not mine but ours'), supports bodies of all sizes and abilities, creates a positive sensory experience, lets teachers work alongside students, and is adjustable on-demand.
- Encourages and supports innovative pedagogy: enables whole-group instruction, choice in partner work, choice in individual worktime, small-group gathering and collaboration, and elicits student voice and the sharing of ideas.

Purpose
The document establishes a shared set of criteria for evaluating and selecting furniture, emphasizing flexibility, student agency, comfort, inclusivity, and support for collaborative, innovative instruction across TSD learning spaces.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
A single-page framework, 'TSD Guiding Principles for Furniture in Future-Ready Learning Environments,' brought to the Troy School District Board of Education as agenda item 8.E at the March 17, 2026 regular meeting. It enumerates five categories of qualities the district seeks in classroom furniture, each with five supporting criteria.

1) Furniture that supports movement and motion: the ability to move around the room easily; partners with other furniture pieces to support multiple configurations; encourages students to move their bodies; allows students to find a comfortable proximity to others; and aids efficient transitions.

2) Furniture that supports and inspires student agency and healthy risk-taking: supports self-awareness in students and is chosen to support learning needs; can be used in many different and even unexpected ways; increases students' ability to sustain engagement; empowers students to show their work; and supports students in their organization and access to tools.

3) Furniture that is comfortable and fosters a sense of belonging: allows students a feeling of safety; is considered comfortable by most; empowers students to work together to organize the furniture purposefully; makes the space feel exciting and joyful; and supports a variety of student postures.

4) Furniture that meets the needs of all students and staff: promotes a sense of community ('not mine but ours'); supports bodies of all sizes and abilities; creates a positive sensory experience; facilitates teachers working alongside students; and is adjustable on-demand.

5) Furniture that encourages and supports innovative pedagogy: provides access to whole-group instruction; choice in partner work; choice in individual worktime; small-group gathering and collaboration; and elicits student voice and the sharing of ideas.

The document is qualitative, containing no dollar figures, vendors, or vote records. It functions as the district's stated rationale and evaluation standard for furniture selection in newly renovated and newly constructed future-ready learning environments.

- Spanish (Klett): $420,153.05

https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
A staff presentation delivered to the Troy School District Board of Education Workshop on April 7, 2026, proposing the adoption of new Levels 1-4 world language instructional resources for Spanish, French, and German. World Languages operate on a 7-year adoption cycle, and the current textbooks have become outdated: Avancemos (2017) for Spanish is out of print with online resources no longer available; T'es Branche (2014) for French contains outdated readings and listening resources and poor organization corrected in newer editions; and Mosaik (2018) for German, used for Levels 1 and 2, has become outdated.

The TSD World Languages vision holds that language learners can communicate in an ever-expanding global community, discover another culture's rich heritage, become resilient risk-takers, improve memory and problem-solving skills, enhance college applications and professional marketability, and open opportunities for world travel.

The selection process was supported by Jen Howe, Oakland Schools Heritage and World Language Consultant. The timeline ran from exploration of resources in 2024-25 through leadership planning (8/11), department kickoff and visioning (8/20), rubric creation and vendor presentations (10/2 and 10/7), pilot planning (10/20), ongoing vendor professional learning and PLC check-ins, pilot feedback and synthesis (3/10), and whole-department unpacking of recommendations (3/20).

Resources considered but not selected were Wayside (French and Spanish, whose content was relatable but included themes that were too specific, with grammar disconnected from themes and inadequate practice) and Klett (French, whose beginning texts were not student-friendly, were poorly organized, and were less engaging).

The chosen resources were: French, Carnegie Learning, cited for significantly updated sequencing, vocabulary, culture, and an online resource bank with pre-AP and scaffolded activities (though upper levels received fewer organizational developments); German, Vista Higher Learning, a familiar, well-organized, fully updated text; and Spanish, Klett, described as proficiency-driven with abundant resources and practice, opportunities for differentiation and inclusivity, authentic student-centered cultural resources, and a strong digital platform integrating communicative activities.

The seven-year financial request totals: Spanish (Klett World Languages) $420,153.05; French (Carnegie Learning) $115,284.96; and German (Vista Higher Learning) $53,049.60. Additional stakeholder input was gathered through French and Spanish student surveys and French and Spanish caretaker surveys.

The anticipated timeline moving forward places the order in July, physical materials inventoried and distributed in early August, and year-long planning with vendors in late August, with systemizing of Levels 1 and 2 during the 2026-27 school year. The presentation included example features such as Spanish 4 students experiencing Carnaval in Colombia and demonstrating understanding through a simulated conversation.

https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.page:
What it is: The draft Troy School District Student Code of Conduct for the 2025-26 school year, presented to the April 7, 2026 Board of Education Workshop. The 16-page document is copyrighted to Miller Johnson School Policy Services.

Purpose: Balances a safe educational environment with the district's duty to serve students who engage in misconduct, while stating it does not limit the district's lawful authority.

Key provisions:
- Acknowledgement: All students and parents must sign an Acknowledgement of Receipt annually at registration, completed through PowerSchool Forms.
- Extracurriculars/Athletics: Participation is a privilege, not a right; athletes are also bound by the TSD Athletic Handbook, acknowledged annually via Final Forms.
- Transportation: Student drivers must be licensed, register, park in designated areas, and consent in advance to vehicle searches; bus riders face loss of transportation privileges for misconduct such as insubordination, smoking/vaping, fighting, profanity, or destruction of property.
- Dress and appearance: Students must wear a shirt (opaque, with a shoulder strap), opaque bottoms, and shoes; prohibited items include violent or drug/alcohol imagery, body armor or tactical gear, hate speech, profanity, pornography, visible undergarments, swimsuits, dangerous accessories, and face-obscuring items (with religious and PPE exceptions).
- Police: The district cooperates with local police in investigations and arrests.

Note: 'Parents' is defined to include legal guardians and those acting in place of parents.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
The draft Troy School District Student Code of Conduct for the 2025-26 school year, prepared for review at the Board of Education Workshop on April 7, 2026. The 16-page document is copyrighted to Miller Johnson School Policy Services and is intended for the sole and exclusive use of Miller Johnson and the Troy School District.

The introduction states that the district must balance the interests of students and the community in a safe and conducive educational environment with its duty to provide educational services to students who engage in misconduct, and that Board of Education policies and this Code are intended to strike that balance without limiting the district's lawful authority. All students and parents must sign the Acknowledgement of Receipt of the Student Code of Conduct annually when students are registered for the school year, completed through PowerSchool Forms. A footnote defines 'parents' to include legal guardians and, where required by law, those acting in the place of parents.

Interscholastic or Extracurricular Activities: Participation in interscholastic or extracurricular athletics is described as a privilege, not a right. Student athletes are subject to the Code at all times as well as additional disciplinary rules in the TSD Athletic Handbook, which parents and athletes must acknowledge annually and digitally through Final Forms.

Transportation: Student drivers must be licensed and receive district permission to park on district property or use their vehicle during the school day; they must register with their school, park only in designated areas, and consent in advance to searches of their vehicles by district personnel at any time, for any reason, with or without notice. Students transported by the district must abide by the driver's direction and the Code; violators face loss of transportation privileges and possible discipline. Cited examples of misconduct include insubordination, smoking/vaping, fighting, profane or foul language, and destruction of property.

Student Dress and Appearance: The primary responsibility for attire resides with the student and parent(s)/guardian(s); dress should respect an inclusive community and not interfere with the health or safety of any student. Students must wear a shirt with opaque fabric and some form of shoulder strap, opaque bottoms (pants/jeans or equivalent such as skirt, sweatpants, leggings, dress, or shorts), and shoes. Students may not wear violent language or images; images or language depicting or suggesting drugs, alcohol, vaping, or paraphernalia; body armor, tactical gear, or facsimile; hate speech, profanity, or pornography; clothing that reveals visible undergarments (visible waistbands and straps are allowed); swimsuits (except as required in class or athletic practice); accessories that could be dangerous or used as a weapon (such as handcuffs or metal accessories); or any item that obscures the face (except for religious observance or PPE such as medical face masks). Hats, hooded sweatshirts, and other head coverings are permitted but must keep the student's face visible to staff. Course-specific attire and footwear requirements (for example, athletic shoes for physical education, closed-toe shoes for science labs and industrial arts) are permitted.

The document also addresses Police Investigations and Arrests, stating that the district cooperates with local police authorities in the interest of the welfare of all citizens and the school.

A slide presentation delivered to the Troy School District Board of Education Workshop in April 2026, reviewing revisions to two governing documents: the Student Code of Conduct and the Athletic Handbook.

Student Code of Conduct: The document was last updated in 2018. The previous version was coupled with student handbook language that was vague and outdated and, when printed, exceeded 70 pages; it was also not aligned to current board policies. The law firm Miller Johnson provides updated board policy guidance for TSD and supplied draft guidelines and a format for the Code of Conduct to align with board policy and administrative regulations. Families will need to sign acknowledgement of the Code of Conduct annually during student enrollment, and the digital document allows for more fluid updates.

Athletic Handbook: The last comprehensive review occurred in 2015. https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.paragraph: A Troy School District secondary math presentation to the April 7, 2026 Board of Education Workshop reviewing the program and recommending a curricular adoption for Geometry and Honors Geometry. After using the same resource for over 15 years, the department piloted OpenUp Mathematics and Illustrative Math (IM) in 2024-25 and IM district-wide in 2025-26, with 100% of Geometry teachers participating. IM, a problem-based curriculum, is recommended and supplemented with printed workbooks and DeltaMath. Teacher perception data from 15 of 16 geometry teachers showed strong confidence alongside noted challenges in parent and struggling-learner supports.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.page:
What it is: A secondary mathematics presentation to the Troy School District Board of Education Workshop on April 7, 2026, on the program review and curricular adoption for Geometry and Honors Geometry.

Framework: Grounded in the Standards for Mathematical Practice, NCTM's 8 Effective Math Teaching Practices (2014), and the TSD Mathematics vision that all students are 'doers of mathematics.'

Current status: The current resource has been used for over 15 years, creating challenges in alignment between teachers and buildings, lacking a coherent storyline, and lacking explicit tools to make learning accessible for all students.

Pilot process:
- 2024-25: Piloted OpenUp Mathematics and Illustrative Math (IM); 70% of Geometry teachers participated. OpenUp was piloted Quarter 1 and discontinued over teacher feedback; IM was piloted Quarters 2-4.
- 2025-26: Piloted IM; 88% of Honors Geometry teachers and 100% of Geometry teachers participated. The Geometry cohort partnered with the Michigan Math and Science Leaders Network (MMSLN).

Recommendation: Adopt Illustrative Math (problem-based, student-centered). IM itself has no cost but is paired with printed workbooks and DeltaMath.

Teacher perception (15 of 16 geometry teachers): 10 of 15 feel confident using IM; 13 of 15 feel confident navigating resources and feel IM advances a problem-based, student-centered curriculum. Challenges: 13 of 15 lack adequate parent-support tools; 12 of 15 feel supports for struggling learners are insufficient. Plans include printed workbooks, DeltaMath, and IM Lesson Summaries and Family Resources on Schoology.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
A secondary mathematics presentation delivered to the Troy School District Board of Education Workshop on April 7, 2026, covering the program review and curricular adoption for Geometry and Honors Geometry. The presentation situates the work within the Standards for Mathematical Practice, make sense of problems and persevere, reason abstractly and quantitatively, construct viable arguments and critique others' reasoning, model with mathematics, use appropriate tools strategically, attend to precision, look for and make use of structure, and look for and express regularity in repeated reasoning, and the eight effective math teaching practices from NCTM (2014). The TSD Mathematics Department's vision, referencing NCTM (2020), holds that all students are doers of mathematics who should develop deep mathematical understandings, understand and critique the world through mathematics, and experience the wonder, joy, and beauty of mathematics.

The department has used its current resource for over 15 years, which presents challenges including alignment between teachers and across buildings, resources organized as topics taught in sequence rather than a storyline that builds conceptual understanding over time, and a lack of explicit tools to make learning accessible for all students. Staff collaborated with districts across the county and national experts and found high school math curriculum options limited and requiring supplementation.

Pilot process: In 2024-25, based on a review matrix, the team piloted OpenUp Mathematics and Illustrative Math (IM), with 70% of Geometry teachers participating; OpenUp was piloted for Quarter 1 and discontinued due to feedback about time constraints, lack of teacher guidance, and explicit practice, while IM was piloted for Quarters 2, 3, and 4 to see the entire story of the year. In 2025-26, the team piloted IM for the full school year, with 88% of Honors Geometry teachers and 100% of Geometry teachers participating. Support included monthly cohort meetings with job-embedded professional learning, and the Geometry cohort partnered with the Michigan Math and Science Leaders Network (MMSLN), which provided professional learning on the IM curriculum, supported prioritizing Geometry standards to create room for pathways such as Statistics, Quantitative Reasoning, or Data Science, and is developing a Data Science module based on Troy teachers' input.

IM is presented as aligning with the district's vision through problem-based, student-centered teaching, with sample SAT and AP exam questions shown. Geometry emphasizes conceptual understanding of proof and application of geometry; Honors Geometry adds conceptual and algebraic application of proof, additional and more advanced trigonometry concepts, project extensions and additional algebra work, and a faster pace.

Teacher perception data (15 of 16 geometry teachers) reported that 10 of 15 feel confident and 3 of 15 somewhat confident using IM; 13 of 15 feel confident navigating IM resources; and 13 of 15 feel IM moves the district toward a problem-based, student-centered curriculum, with teachers praising its focus on the 'why' behind the math, student discussion, and storyline. Challenges reported: 13 of 15 feel they lack adequate sample communications and tools to provide parents with at-home support, addressed by a printed workbook, extra practice with DeltaMath, and IM Lesson Summaries and Family Resources posted on Schoology; and 12 of 15 feel the tools provided to support struggling learners are not sufficient.

What it is: A March 2026 Board of Education update on middle school mathematics, summarizing implementation progress and survey feedback for the district's new math curriculum (Illustrative Mathematics), adopted May 2023 to replace the former Big Ideas materials.

Background and commitments: The district cited outdated materials and misalignment with its math vision. Administration committed to annual review of achievement data (MSTEP/PSAT) and course-enrollment data (Honors Algebra 1), annual staff/student/family feedback, NWEA implementation, ongoing teacher support, and MTSS structures. The Board committed to reviewing annual data on a 3-5 year implementation timeline, noting adoption need not follow a full 7-year cycle if concerns arise.

Achievement data: MSTEP was reviewed for 6th grade (2024 first-year and 2025 second-year implementation) and 7th grade (2025 first-year); 8th-grade PSAT data for 2026 (the first fully implemented cohort) is not yet available.

Enrollment: 8th-grade enrollment in honors math (Algebra 1 and above) rose across cohorts (reported totals 907, 961, 995, 1,023), attributed to the middle school math sequence change.

Survey participation: Student survey 2,059 (72%), Parent/Guardian survey 398 (14%), Staff survey 21 (81%). Students and parents reported a mix of feeling appropriately leveled, underchallenged, or lost.

Staff-identified improvement areas (n=21): Too Much Content in Honors Algebra 1 combined with Math 8 (7; 33.3%), Difficulty with Differentiation/pacing/learning gaps/supports (5; 23.8%), Underchallenged Students (5; 23.8%), and Fear of Lower Outcomes for Algebra 1 Students (4; 19.0%).

Purpose: To give the Board data-informed feedback on curriculum implementation and areas needing attention within the current math progression model.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
Presented to the Troy School District Board of Education in the March/April 2026 cycle, this middle school math update ('MS Math Update -- Survey Feedback, March 2026') reviews the progress of the district's new mathematics curriculum and progression. Historical context notes that former materials (Big Ideas) were outdated and did not align to the district's vision for math, leading the Board to adopt a new curriculum and new progression in May 2023, built around Illustrative Mathematics.

The update restates commitments made at adoption. TSD Administration committed to: annual review of student achievement data (MSTEP/PSAT); annual review of student course-enrollment data (Honors Algebra 1); annual collection of feedback from staff, students, and families; implementation of NWEA; investment in ongoing teacher support; and continuing to build MTSS structures to support student growth. The Board of Education committed to reviewing annual data sets, understanding the implementation timeline, and recognizing a 3-5 year implementation timeline, noting that adoption does not require a full 7-year cycle if other concerns arise. A curriculum adoption and implementation cycle is described in phases -- Research & Vision, Explore, and Implementation -- within an ongoing Curriculum Review Cycle involving teacher/administrator review teams, pilots and early-adopter classrooms, professional learning, coaching, and site visits.

On academic achievement, the district has annually reviewed MSTEP data for 6th and 7th grades: MSTEP 6th grade 2024 (first year of implementation data) and 2025 (second year), and MSTEP 7th grade 2025 (first year). No 8th-grade PSAT achievement data is available yet for 2026, the first cohort to experience full implementation of the new program. Reported n-values include 567, 607, 643, 576, 642, and 677.

Enrollment trends show that the middle school math sequence change led to an increase in 8th-grade student enrollment in honors math courses (Algebra 1 and above), with total students reported across cohorts as 907, 961, 995, and 1,023; the district will continue to monitor these enrollments.

The district administered a perception survey to middle school students, parents/guardians, and math teachers covering instructional practices, implementation of Illustrative Mathematics, student learning, and course progression. Participation was: Student Survey 2,059 responses (72% of population), Parent/Guardian Survey 398 (14%), and Staff Survey 21 (81%). Sample student/parent response options ranged from understanding lesson goals because the work is at the right level, to feeling underchallenged and wanting more advanced work, to feeling lost even after asking questions. Among staff (n=21), 7 (33.3%) said most students understand lesson goals, 7 (33.3%) said most students feel lost, and 1 (4.8%) said most students are underchallenged, with additional mixed combinations reported.

The staff survey identified the main themes needing to be addressed within the current math progression model: Too Much Content in Honors Algebra 1 (combined with Math 8) -- 7 responses (33.3%); Difficulty with Differentiation, including pacing, learning gaps, and student supports -- 5 (23.8%); Underchallenged Students -- 5 (23.8%); and Fear of Lower Outcomes for Algebra 1 Students -- 4 (19.0%).

https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.paragraph: A March 9, 2026 policy update memo from MJ School Policy Services (Miller Johnson) to client districts, including Troy, recommending substantive revisions to policy manuals. The two Students-series updates are Update 22.01 to Policy 2003 (Education Records), adding student-survey requirements under MCL 388.1764k / Section 164k of the FY2026 State School Aid Act, and Update 22.02 to Policy 2004 (Extracurricular Activities), addressing the MHSAA's January 23, 2026 expansion of personal branding activity (PBA) / name, image, and likeness (NIL) rules for student-athletes.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.page:
What it is: A March 9, 2026 policy and administrative-regulation update memorandum from MJ School Policy Services (the Miller Johnson law firm) to its policy-service client districts, including Troy School District. It presents recommended, individually numbered revisions (e.g., Update 22.01) by policy section, with additions shown in red and deletions in blue.

Sections with no updates: Introduction (0000) and Bylaws (1000).

Students series (2000):
- Update 22.01 (Policy 2003, Education Records): Adds requirements from MCL 388.1764k, enacted in the FY2026 State School Aid Act (Section 164k), governing student surveys. Parents may inspect all survey/analysis/evaluation materials tied to U.S. Department of Education-funded programs, and student participation in surveys revealing sensitive topics (political/religious beliefs, mental or psychological problems, sexual behavior, self-incriminating behavior, family appraisals, privileged relationships, or income) requires parental consent. The district must post questions and results of district-wide, state/federally mandated, and grade-level surveys on its website and notify parents, while complying with FERPA before releasing results.
- Update 22.02 (Policy 2004, Extracurricular Activities): Applies to MHSAA member districts. Reflects the MHSAA's January 23, 2026 expansion of its personal branding activities (PBA) / name, image, or likeness (NIL) rule (Regulation I, Section 11 C -- Amateur Status/Awards), which lets students earn NIL compensation regardless of athletics. The added language prohibits PBA/NIL agreements that violate Board Policy or the Student Code of Conduct and bars such activities during school hours or events or on school property.

Purpose: To keep client districts' policy manuals compliant with new Michigan law and MHSAA rules. Contact: Policy@MillerJohnson.com.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
This memorandum, dated March 9, 2026, is from MJ School Policy Services (a service of the Miller Johnson law firm) to its policy-service client districts, which include Troy School District, and conveys recommended substantive updates to all MJ School Policy Services policy and administrative-regulation manuals. The memo explains its conventions: updates are numbered individually (for example, Update 22.01); additions to policy or administrative-regulation language are shown in red, deletions in blue, and yellow-highlighted areas require additional information from the district. Because each district's manual is unique, some recommended changes may already be present; questions are directed to Policy@MillerJohnson.com, and districts behind on updates are urged to seek compliance support.

By section, the Introduction (0000 Series) and Bylaws (1000 Series) have no recommended updates. The substantive changes fall in the Students (2000) Series.

Update 22.01 revises Policy 2003, Education Records. The fiscal year 2026 State School Aid Act includes MCL 388.1764k, which adds requirements for school districts and intermediate school districts regarding student surveys; the update is recommended to ensure compliance with Section 164k. Miller Johnson references its guidance titled 'New Compliance Requirements Under Section 164k -- State School Aid Act (FY 2025-2026)' and 'Additional Guidance on Section 164k Compliance -- District Surveys & Curriculum Requirements.' The revised policy language provides that parents may inspect all materials used for any student survey, analysis, or evaluation conducted in connection with a U.S. Department of Education-funded program, and that the district will not, without parental consent, require a student to participate in a survey, analysis, or evaluation that reveals information concerning: political or religious affiliations, beliefs, or practices; mental or psychological problems; sexual behavior or attitudes; illegal, anti-social, self-incriminating, or demeaning behavior; critical appraisals of individuals with close family relationships; legally recognized privileged relationships (such as with lawyers, physicians, and ministers); or income (except when required by law to determine program or financial-assistance eligibility). In compliance with MCL 388.1764k, the district will make questions and results of district-wide, state- or federally mandated, and grade-level surveys available to the public by posting them on the district website and notifying parents, while complying with the Family Educational Rights and Privacy Act (FERPA) before releasing any survey results.

Update 22.02 revises Policy 2004, Extracurricular Activities, and applies to districts that are members of the Michigan High School Athletic Association (MHSAA). The MHSAA approved an expansion of its personal branding activities (PBA) / name, image, or likeness (NIL) rule -- Regulation I, Section 11 C -- Amateur Status/Awards -- on January 23, 2026. Effective immediately, a student may earn compensation through their PBA (use of their NIL), such as promoting or endorsing a product or service, regardless of whether the PBA relates to athletics. The added policy language is intended to prohibit students from engaging in PBA/NIL agreements that violate Board Policy or the Student Code of Conduct and to provide additional protections for the district; students may be disciplined for violations. The policy also directs the Superintendent, in consultation with the Board and selected personnel, to administer interscholastic athletics under the principle that participants are students first and athletes second, and specifies that PBA/NIL activities shall not occur during school hours or events or on School District property.

https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
This is the text of Troy School District Board Policy 8001, Acceptable Use, within the district's General Policies (8000 Series), as presented at the April 7, 2026 Board of Education workshop. The policy states that School District students and staff members may be permitted access to the School District's computer network for educational, instructional, and administrative purposes. It directs the Superintendent to develop and implement guidelines and user agreements that are consistent with the purposes and mission of the School District, and specifies that these guidelines and user agreements will include all requirements of the Children's Internet Protection Act (CIPA). More particularly, the policy requires that provisions be made for monitoring the online activities of minors and for educating minors about appropriate online behavior.

The policy includes an Artificial Intelligence section, the substantive addition of this revision. It provides that the Superintendent may develop administrative regulations governing the use of generative artificial intelligence, large language models, or other similar technology. It further notes that such administrative regulations may consider data privacy, training, acceptable use, and student use of such technology. The policy thus establishes board-level authority for the Superintendent to regulate AI use through administrative regulation, rather than prescribing detailed AI rules in the policy itself.

A resolution of the Board of Education of the Troy School District, Oakland County, Michigan, titled 'Resolution Declaring the Necessity to Acquire Highway and Sidewalk Easements and to Authorize Clark Hill PLC to Institute Condemnation Proceedings to Acquire Easements.' It is framed for adoption at a special Board meeting held at 4420 Livernois Road, Troy, Michigan 48098-4799 on April 7, 2026 at 7:00 p.m., with fields for present/absent members and the moving and supporting members left blank in this draft.

Background recitals: The District, a Michigan general powers school district, is undertaking construction and operation of the new Smith Middle School on Livernois Road, a project that includes roadway and sidewalk improvements for public benefit, safety, mobility, and accessibility. As part of the project the District must construct driveway approaches and a deceleration lane on the east side of Livernois Road, widen the road, and add traffic-signal and sidewalk improvements (the 'Livernois Road Improvements'). To do so it must acquire permanent highway and sidewalk easements over property owned by Mirza Azam-Ali Baig and Juveria Baig, husband and wife, commonly known as 5836 Livernois Road, Tax Parcel No. 20-10-101-033. The easements are set out in a Declaration of Necessity and Taking of Property attached as Exhibit A. Negotiations with the owners were not successful.

Legal authority recited: Section 11a of the Revised School Code (Public Act 451 of 1976, MCL 380.11a) empowers the District to acquire real-property interests by condemnation under the Uniform Condemnation Procedures Act (Public Act 87 of 1980, MCL 213.51 et seq.). The District reserves the right to bring federal or state cost-recovery actions against the owner for any release of hazardous or toxic substances on the easement. The District will first present a good-faith written offer based on an appraisal by a state-certified appraiser; if rejected, Clark Hill PLC is authorized to file a condemnation lawsuit.

Operative resolutions: (1) The Board declares the Project a public improvement and finds it necessary and essential to acquire the easements in, on, over, under, across, and through the Property for the Livernois Road Improvements, which benefit the public and improve public safety. (2) The Board authorizes the Superintendent of Schools — or, in his absence, the Deputy Superintendent of Business Affairs — to take all action and execute all documents necessary under the Revised School Code, the UCPA, and other applicable law, including acquiring the easements, recording the Statement of Necessity and Declaration of Taking (Exhibit A), retaining qualified appraisers or consultants to determine just compensation, making good-faith written offers to owners, negotiating and reaching agreement on just compensation, and initiating condemnation proceedings in the Oakland County Circuit Court. (3) The Deputy Superintendent of Business Affairs is authorized to establish an escrow account with First American Title Company for the specific estimated just-compensation amounts. (4) Clark Hill PLC is retained as counsel, with substitute counsel permitted if a conflict arises. This is the companion resolution to the Statement of Public Necessity and Declaration of Taking for the same Baig property; the estimated just compensation stated in related documents is approximately $6,600 total.

- Symptoms and characteristics may present in a variety of combinations and can result in significant, lifelong challenges affecting learning, daily living, employment, social-interactive behaviors, and understanding of verbal and nonverbal communication.
- As efforts to address autism continue, physicians, psychologists, behavior analysts, speech and language pathologists, occupational therapists, vocational rehabilitation professionals, and educators can assist persons with autism and their families by supporting early identification, education, intervention, recreation, and other opportunities vital to development and well-being.
- The Troy School District is honored to celebrate the ways individuals with autism enhance the school community and is committed to fostering acceptance and a sense of belonging to create a more welcoming and inclusive environment for all.

The operative clause reads: 'NOW, BE IT THEREFORE RESOLVED, that the Board of Education hereby recognizes April 2026 as Autism Acceptance Month in the Troy School District.' The document closes with blank Yes and No lines for recording the vote. It is a ceremonial proclamation and carries no budgetary or contractual content.

https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
A workshop slide deck titled 'Troy School District Student Code of Conduct & Athletic Handbook,' presented at the April 2026 Board of Education Workshop, walking the board through proposed revisions to two governing documents.

Student Code of Conduct: The current Code was last updated in 2018. The presentation characterizes the existing document as coupled with student-handbook language that was vague and outdated, and lengthy—printed at more than 70 pages. The proposed replacement is specific to Code of Conduct guidelines and aligned to current board policies, which the prior document was not. The law firm Miller Johnson provides updated board-policy guidance for TSD and supplied draft guidelines and a format for the Code of Conduct that aligns with board policy and administrative regulations. The document was developed by Miller Johnson and refined by a TSD team, then vetted by K-12 building principals, assistant principals, the supervisor for wellness and community engagement, and central office leaders. Key changes include succinct language for clearer expectations; the addition of 'discriminatory harassment' as a category to capture data on student behaviors; updated processes and language aligned to Michigan laws and adopted board policies; restorative language throughout; alignment of Code language to PowerSchool for improved data collection; an annual family acknowledgement signed during student enrollment; and a digital format allowing more fluid updates.

Athletic Handbook: The handbook last received a comprehensive review in 2015. It has been renamed 'Athletic Handbook' to avoid confusion with the Code of Conduct. The revision is aligned to MHSAA rules and guidelines, TSD board policies and administrative regulations, and district values and educational mission, with clarified expectations for coaches, athletes, and families, and includes new sections and content that did not previously exist. Stakeholder input was collected through surveys and individual conversations representing more than 50 individuals—student-athletes, coaches, parents, athletic coordinators, and building administrators. New sections include High School NIL (Name, Image, Likeness) guidelines, a Student Athlete Disciplinary Framework, and Season Expectations.

Future work anticipated for the 2026-27 school year includes updating the CAP Pact (Coach-Athlete-Parent) and developing additional guidelines specific to middle school sports. The deck functions as an informational review supporting eventual board adoption of both documents; it names no dollar amounts or votes.

- Frames athletics as an extension of the classroom supporting social-emotional learning, responsibility, teamwork, leadership, and time management
- Operates under the umbrella of the TSD Student Code of Conduct; Code violations trigger the handbook's disciplinary procedures
- In effect year-round; academically ineligible athletes may still practice unless under school suspension, but may lose award eligibility
- Policies marked with an asterisk (*) are TSD-adopted and also align with MHSAA regulations

- II Awards; III Maintaining Amateur Status; IV Outside-of-School Competition

Purpose: The governing rulebook draft for TSD interscholastic athletics, presented for board review.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
The draft 'Athletic Handbook for Students,' revised Spring 2026, is the Troy School District's comprehensive rulebook for interscholastic athletic participation, presented to the Board of Education. The extracted text captures the full table of contents and the introduction.

The handbook is organized into fifteen sections. Section I, Rules of Eligibility for Participation, covers Enrollment, Age, the Parent/Guardian and Student-Athlete FinalForms account, Participant Physical Examination, Seasons of Competition, Semester of Eligibility, and Academic Eligibility under Troy School District requirements. Section II covers Awards; Section III, Maintaining Amateur Status; Section IV, Outside of School Athletic Competition; Section V, Student Attendance Required for Athletics; and Section VI, Attendance at Athletic Practice Sessions and Contests. Section VII sets Season Expectations for Players, Parents, and Coaches, including the Troy CAP Pact. Section VIII addresses Traveling to and from Away Contests; Section IX, Uniforms and Equipment; and Section X, Use or Possession of Tobacco, Alcohol and Other Drug Substances. Section XI covers Summer and Off-Season Programs; Section XII, Name-Image-Likeness / Personal Branding Activity; Section XIII, Supplemental Rules and Regulations; Section XIV, the Student-Athlete Handbook Disciplinary Framework; and Section XV, Appeal Procedures.

The introduction states that the handbook is designed to provide a consistent framework of expectations, responsibilities, and guidelines for all student-athletes, regardless of the team or school they represent, and that it integrates the rules and regulations of the Michigan High School Athletic Association (MHSAA) as adopted by the district, along with district-specific policies governing interscholastic athletic participation. Athletics are framed as a vital extension of the classroom—an opportunity to develop social-emotional learning, personal responsibility, teamwork, leadership, time management, and athletic skill—complementing academic achievement.

The handbook operates under the umbrella of the Troy School District Student Code of Conduct; any student-athlete who violates the Code is also subject to the disciplinary procedures outlined in the handbook. The handbook is in effect throughout the entire year, including all seasons of practice and competition, and continued eligibility is described as a privilege dependent on adherence to all of its components. A student-athlete deemed academically ineligible for contests or scrimmages may still practice with the team provided they are not under school suspension, though inability to compete may affect eligibility for athletic awards as determined by team-specific requirements set by the coach and communicated at the start of each season. Policies marked with an asterisk (*) are those adopted by Troy School District that also align with MHSAA regulations, and student-athletes are subject to all current MHSAA rules whether or not those rules are explicitly detailed in the handbook. The document is a draft presented for the board's review at the April 21, 2026 meeting.

https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
A memorandum from the Troy School District Operations Department (1140 Rankin, Troy, MI 48083), dated March 26, 2026, from Rob Carson, Director of Maintenance & Operations, to Dan Trudel, Assistant Superintendent of Business Services, recommending contract awards under Bid 2526-28 for THS Classroom Renovations, Baker Middle Vestibule Renovation, and the Barnard & Bemis Operable Wall Replacement Project.

An RFP was issued for competitive bids to perform two special education classroom renovations and an operable wall in the staff lounge (Alternate 1) at Troy High School, a renovation to the entrance vestibule at Baker Middle School, and the purchase and installation of new operable partition walls at Barnard and Bemis Elementary Schools. LMS Construction was the low qualified bidder, including Alternate 1. Gardiner Vose, Inc. was the low recommended bidder for the operable partition category; although not the absolute low bid, its operable wall selection matches four other operable walls already in the district and is preferred for standardization. Post-bids were conducted by Lecole Planners to verify the accuracy and thoroughness of the contractor bids.

The recommended awards are: General Construction to LMS Construction (base bid including Alternate 1) at $271,997.00; and Operable Partition to Gardiner Vose, Inc. (including Alternate 1) at $137,225.79. An 8% contingency of $32,737.82 is added for unforeseen circumstances, yielding a total recommended award of $441,960.61. Carson requests approval of this total project cost, noting a separate purchase order will be issued to each contractor upon approval.

Funding for the purchase will come from the Building Site & Sinking Fund, and the intent is to perform the work over summer break. The memo was copied to Donna Havrilla of the Business Department and to the Purchasing Department file.

https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
Board of Education Policy 8000.01 - Acceptable Use, presented in revised form at the April 21, 2026 Regular Meeting. The policy establishes that Troy School District students and staff members may be permitted access to the school district's computer network for educational, instructional, and administrative purposes.

Under the policy, the Superintendent will develop and implement guidelines and user agreements that are consistent with the purposes and mission of the school district. These guidelines and user agreements will include all requirements of the Children's Internet Protection Act (CIPA). More particularly, provision is to be made for monitoring the online activities of minors and for educating minors about appropriate online behavior.

The revision adds a new section addressing artificial intelligence. It provides that the Superintendent may develop administrative regulations governing generative artificial intelligence, large language models, or other similar technology, and that such administrative regulations may consider data privacy, training, acceptable use, and student use of such technology.

A tracked editorial comment in the document, attributed to the initials DT, explains that the language was added to the policy to address the need for additional administrative regulation regarding AI, and that this updated regulation was presented to the Board at the March workshop. The policy thereby serves two purposes: it authorizes and frames network access for students and staff while ensuring CIPA compliance, and it creates an explicit basis for the Superintendent to issue administrative regulations covering the district's use of generative AI and large language models. The policy text is high-level, delegating specific operational rules to Superintendent-developed guidelines, user agreements, and administrative regulations rather than spelling them out in the policy itself.

Recognitions: The Board honored students selected for the Michigan School Band and Orchestra Association (MSBOA) All-State Ensembles, which perform at the annual Michigan Music Conference in Grand Rapids at DeVos Performance Hall; the blind selection process is highly competitive, with roughly 2,500 students competing for about 400 seats. Orchestra teacher Claire Murphy introduced the honorees. All-State Orchestra: Gabriella Murphy, Chloe Kim, Junghwan Kim, Ryeo-Won Kim, Yuna Kim, Leon Ma, and Ariel Song. All-State Jazz Band: Ryan Deller (lead tenor sax) and Brad Zapatka (lead alto sax).

TSD Mission Moment: Students from Adam Burns' class at Athens produced the documentary short "Why Native Plants?" for an environmental journalism project funded by a grant from the Knight Center for Journalism at Michigan State University, aimed at incorporating more native plants into school grounds and curriculum. The film won the Michigan Award at the Coastline Children's Film Festival, was featured by Wild Ones and Rochester Pollinators, and was the first Michigan film selected for the United Nations' Youth Climate Report. Presenting students were Cecelia Gould, Olivia Lee, and Samantha Sanday.

Consent Agenda: Moved by Haupt and supported by Potts, the Board approved items A through F by a 7-0 vote: minutes of the February 3, 2026 Board Workshop; minutes of the February 24, 2026 Board meeting; the January 2026 Treasurer's Report; Budget Amendment #2; Schools Closed to Open Enrollment; and Sex Education Advisory Board (SEAB) membership approval.

https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.paragraph: A March 2026 policy-update memo from MJ School Policy Services (Miller Johnson) recommending substantive revisions to the district's policy manual and administrative regulations. The headline change — Update 22.01 to Policy 2003, Education Records — implements new MCL 388.1764k / §164k student-survey requirements from the FY2025–26 State School Aid Act: parental inspection rights, opt-in consent for sensitive surveys, and public posting of survey questions and results, subject to FERPA.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.page:
Source & format
A memo (dated March 9, 2026) from MJ School Policy Services to policy clients, delivering substantive updates to the policy manual and administrative regulations. Revisions are organized by manual section with individually numbered updates (e.g., Update 22.01); additions are shown in red, deletions in blue, and yellow highlights flag items needing district-specific input.

Headline update — 22.01, Policy 2003 (Education Records)
The FY2025–26 State School Aid Act adds MCL 388.1764k, imposing new student-survey requirements on districts and ISDs. Recommended revisions ensure compliance with §164k:
• Parents may inspect all materials used for any student survey, analysis, or evaluation tied to a U.S. Department of Education–funded program.
• Without parental consent, students may not be required to take surveys revealing sensitive information (political/religious beliefs, mental health, sexual behavior, self-incriminating behavior, privileged relationships, income, etc.).
• Questions and results of district-wide, state/federally mandated, and grade-level surveys must be posted publicly on the district website, with parent notification — subject to FERPA before any release.

Other updates
Update 22.02 revises Policy 2004 (Extracurricular Activities); additional numbered updates follow across policy sections.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
What this is
This document is the March 2026 policy-and-administrative-regulations update memo from MJ School Policy Services (a Miller Johnson service), addressed to policy-service clients and dated March 9, 2026. It is a standardized vendor product: proposed revisions are presented by manual section, each with an individual update number for reference, accompanied by narrative explaining the basis for each change. The memo notes its editing conventions — additions to policy or AR language are shown in red, deletions in blue, and passages highlighted in yellow require additional district-specific information to complete. It cautions that, because each district's manuals are customized, some recommendations may already be reflected locally.

Students — 2000 Series
Update 22.01 (Policy 2003, Education Records). The fiscal year 2026 State School Aid Act includes MCL 388.1764k, adding requirements for districts and ISDs regarding student surveys; adopting the revisions ensures compliance with Section 164k. Miller Johnson's supporting guidance is cited (“New Compliance Requirements Under Section 164k” and “Additional Guidance on Section 164k Compliance — District Surveys & Curriculum Requirements”). Substantively: parents may inspect all materials used for any student survey, analysis, or evaluation conducted in connection with a U.S. Department of Education–funded program; and the district will not, without parental consent, require a student to participate in a survey, analysis, or evaluation that reveals information concerning the student's or parents' political or religious affiliations/beliefs/practices; mental or psychological problems; sexual behavior or attitudes; illegal, anti-social, self-incriminating, or demeaning behavior; critical appraisals of individuals with close family relationships; legally recognized privileged relationships (lawyers, physicians, ministers); or income (except where required by law to determine program eligibility). In compliance with MCL 388.1764k, the district will make the questions and results of district-wide, state- or federally-mandated, and grade-level surveys available to the public by posting them on the district website and notifying parents — while complying with FERPA before releasing any survey results.

Other sections
The Introduction (0000) and Bylaws (1000) series have no recommended updates. Update 22.02 addresses Policy 2004 (Extracurricular Activities), with further numbered updates continuing through the manual. Districts behind on updates are urged to contact the firm (Policy@MillerJohnson.com) for compliance support.

The subject line is "Policy Manual and Administrative Regulations Update - October 2025." The Troy School District included this memo in its board packet to support consideration of a facility dog policy.

The memo's central substantive recommendation is Update 21.03, marked *NEW*, introducing Policy 6013 (Facility Dog). MJ notes that in recent months several client districts had expressed interest in having a facility dog in a school building, and that this is different from allowing service animals pursuant to the Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA). Facility dogs - often called therapy dogs - are animals brought in by the school for general use by the student population, and are described as School District-owned dogs trained to work within school facilities and at school events with children who have a variety of academic, social, and emotional needs. MJ recommends adopting the new facility dog policy if a district plans to obtain or use a facility dog. Under the recommended policy, the Superintendent would promulgate an administrative regulation applicable to the use of facility dogs on School District property. The item is placed within the Facilities and Operations 6000 Series. An embedded editorial comment ("[DT1]") reiterates the recommendation to adopt a formal policy regarding facility dogs for future use, noting that if a policy is needed an official Administrative Regulation would be made.

The memo also carries administrative and platform news. Updates to clients' online policy sites were to begin the week of November 3, 2025, without downtime; the update would provide a new interface and added features, including the ability to download and print policies and to translate policies and administrative regulations into another language. New URLs for policy sites were still forthcoming, with current sites automatically redirecting to the new URL to ensure continuity of service. MJ explains its editing conventions: additions to policy or administrative-regulation language are shown in red, deletions in blue, and areas highlighted in yellow require additional information from the district. Evaluation and outcome
- Rubric phases: Phase 1 The Reading League, Phase 2 EdReports, Phase 3 ESSA, aligned to a TSD vision and pillars.

https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose: A K-8 Literacy Curriculum Review Update presentation delivered to the Troy School District Board of Education on April 28, 2026, anchored in the Science of Reading and Structured Literacy. The deck opens with an overview of the components of Michigan's Public Act 146: assessments, Multi-Tiered Systems of Support, literacy coaching, professional learning, English Learners, and suggested Tier 1 elementary reading curricula, and situates Troy's K-8 Tier 1 pilot within the MDE timeline. The district review process began by establishing a Curriculum Review Committee comprising the literacy leadership team, classroom teachers, literacy specialists, ELD specialists, special education teachers, principals, and district administrators. A data-review phase examined aggregate national, state, county, and district trends (citing the NAEP Reading Assessment), TSD's current subgroup data, and perception data from staff, families, and students. K-5 staff valued responsive teaching, small-group instruction, intervention, book clubs, and high-engagement choice-and-voice curriculum, while recommending more explicit phonics and vocabulary instruction; K-5 families praised literacy growth and book bags/clubs but wanted stronger phonics, spelling, and decoding, plus more take-home materials. At grades 6-8, staff endorsed student choice with novels and peer dialogue but sought more whole-class novels, assessment-supporting materials, and task scaffolding, while families wanted more grammar, spelling, and vocabulary instruction. Shared learning drew on Oakland Schools (PA 146 Leadership Series, Instructional Leadership Network, MTSS Handbook, structured-literacy and dyslexia sessions, and ongoing consultant work) and an MDE LETRS training cohort, plus visits from 14 curriculum vendors and district site visits to Novi and Birmingham (Arts and Letters), South Lyon (Collaborative Classroom and UFLI), and West Bloomfield (EL Education). Research highlights cited include work by Nell Duke, Mark Seidenberg, Robert J. Tierney and P. David Pearson, Timothy Shanahan, and Katherine Marsh's Atlantic piece Why Kids Aren't Falling in Love with Reading. Evaluation used MDE rubrics across three phases - Phase 1 The Reading League, Phase 2 EdReports, and Phase 3 ESSA (Every Student Succeeds Act) - alongside TSD rubrics aligned to the district's literacy vision and pillars. In the K-5 comprehensive-curriculum reviewer scoring (2-Strong, 1-Moderate, 0-Weak by pillar), Collaborative Literacy was the overwhelming preference at 96%, HMH Into Reading at 4%, and Arts and Letters, EL Education, SAVVAS, and CKLA each at 0%. Collaborative Literacy is described as a comprehensive, evidence-based K-5 program integrating foundational skills, comprehension, and knowledge-building, with The Reading League noting its coverage of Scarborough's Reading Rope elements. The presentation also incorporates the district's K-8 Literacy Vision Statement, which commits to a cohesive framework balancing high-volume reading, strong foundational skills, differentiated instruction, and student choice and voice.

https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose: A blank curriculum-review scoring rubric used by Troy School District to evaluate grades 6-8 curricular resources, with header fields for the curricular resource name, reviewer name, and building. The instrument is organized around the district's four strategic pillars, each carrying a maximum point value: Equity and Well-Being (scored out of 5), Early Childhood to Career (out of 3), Deep Learning (out of 8), and Building Capacity (out of 4). Equity and Well-Being is defined as ensuring all students experience the academic, social, and emotional support they need to reach their potential, and its guiding questions ask how the curriculum values student identities, backgrounds, and cultures; supports differentiation for all learners including ELD and Special Education students; provides extension opportunities for gifted learners; embeds actionable Tier 2 supports; and sets appropriate boundaries around screen time. Early Childhood to Career covers learning opportunities from a child's earliest years through graduation to adulthood, asking whether the curriculum fosters student joy in reading and writing, provides clear vertical alignment across grade levels, and demonstrates cohesive alignment within and across units. Deep Learning is framed around developing lifelong skills - critical thinking, collaboration, character, creativity, citizenship, and communication - and its questions address the use of rich mentor texts, high-interest read-alouds, and varied student texts; incorporation of student voice, choice, and personal connection; coverage of the breadth of the Common Core State Standards in reading, writing, listening, and speaking; levels of rigor that support striving readers while advancing gifted learners; teaching of foundational skills such as morphology, vocabulary, comprehension, and fluency; inclusion of a range of text types (full novels, short stories, excerpts, anthologies, and physical books); and opportunities for student assessment and teacher responsiveness. Building Capacity concerns providing regular opportunities for staff and families to learn from one another and from local, state, and global partnerships, asking whether the curriculum is user-friendly to implement and assess, easy to onboard for new teachers, systemic while allowing professional decision-making, and supported by targeted, effective professional development and collaboration. The rubric closes with an Evidence field for each of the four pillars and a corresponding score line (Score ___/5, ___/3, ___/8, and ___/4).

https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose: A blank elementary reading curriculum review rubric used by Troy School District to evaluate K-5 resources, with reviewers scoring on a three-point scale of 2 (Strong), 1 (Moderate), or 0 (Weak). The rubric is organized around four color-coded district pillars. The Blue pillar, Deep Learning, is defined as deepening learning with a commitment to lifelong skills such as critical thinking, collaboration, character, creativity, citizenship, and communication. The Red pillar, Equity and Well-Being, focuses on ensuring all students experience the academic, social, and emotional support they need to reach their potential. The Gold pillar, Building Capacity, concerns providing regular opportunities for staff and families to learn from one another and from local, state, and global partnerships. The Green pillar, Early Childhood to Career, addresses learning opportunities designed to educate and support children from their earliest years through graduation to adulthood. Under these pillars the rubric poses numerous guiding questions: how the curriculum presents opportunities for deep learning and supports all students in engaging with the Michigan standards for literacy; whether it allows student talk, choice, voice, feedback, oral rehearsal, and a large volume of reading; whether it provides a systematic framework including explicit instruction, shared practice, independent practice, and small-group differentiated instruction; how it is cohesively sequenced in a storyline or learning arc that spirals over time and revisits skills; how it uses rich mentor texts, high-interest read-alouds, and a variety of student texts while limiting screen time; how it elicits high engagement by valuing student ideas, connecting to identities, and ensuring opportunities for all; how it supports differentiation through explicit instruction and varied materials; whether it represents diverse backgrounds and perspectives through mentor and student texts; how it promotes student voice and an inclusive, asset-based learning environment; how teachers are supported through ongoing, timely, job-embedded professional learning and unit unpacking; the scope, sequence, and variety of that professional learning; how the curriculum supports implementation, materials access, and differentiation; whether it reflects the diverse community it serves; how it partners with families and community and offers reading for extended audiences; how it connects to a peer-reviewed research base or learning organization; how it aligns Pre-K through 12th grade to future pathways and aspirations; how it prioritizes high-volume reading with clear purpose to deepen comprehension and motivation; how it uses intentional scaffolding for transitions across grade levels and home/school connections; how it elicits a lifelong joy of reading; and what learning and assessment opportunities show reading growth across K-5. Each of the four pillars concludes with an Evidence field and an Overall rating/impression line.

https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose: A Middle School Math Update presentation delivered to the Troy School District Board of Education on April 28, 2026, centered on March 2026 survey feedback about the district's middle-school math curriculum. In historical context, the presentation notes the former curriculum, Big Ideas, had outdated materials that did not align to the district's vision for math, and that the Board adopted a new curriculum and new progression in May 2023. The new program is Illustrative Mathematics. The deck lays out commitments made at adoption: TSD administration committed to annual review of student achievement data (MSTEP/PSAT), annual review of student course enrollment data (Honors Algebra 1), annual collection of feedback from staff, students, and families, implementation of NWEA, investment in ongoing teacher support, and continued building of MTSS structures; the Board of Education committed to reviewing annual data sets, understanding the implementation timeline, recognizing a 3-5 year implementation timeline, and acknowledging that adoption does not require a full 7-year cycle if other concerns arise. It also describes the district's Curriculum Review Cycle phases of Explore, Research & Vision, and Implementation. On academic achievement, the district reports it has annually reviewed MSTEP data for 6th and 7th grade, specifically MSTEP 6th grade 2024 (first year of implementation data), MSTEP 6th grade 2025 (second year of 6th grade implementation data), and MSTEP 7th grade 2025 (first year of implementation data); PSAT 8th grade 2026 has no academic achievement data available yet because that is the first cohort to have full implementation of the new program. Cohort n-values shown include 567, 607, and 643, and 576, 642, and 677. A slide on 8th grade enrollment trends in honors math courses (Algebra 1 and above) reports that the middle school math sequence change led to an increase in student enrollment in honors, with total student counts displayed as 907, 961, 995, and 1,023 across successive years, and states the district will continue to monitor honors enrollments. The district administered a survey to middle school students, parents/guardians, and math teachers to gather feedback on instructional practices, implementation of Illustrative Mathematics, student learning, and course progression. Participation was 2,059 students (72% of the population), 398 parents/guardians (14%), and 21 staff (81%). Sample student responses ranged from understanding lesson goals because work is at the right level, to feeling underchallenged and wanting more advanced work, to feeling lost even after asking questions. From the teacher perspective (n=21), 7 (33.3%) agreed most students understand the lesson goals, 7 (33.3%) said most students feel lost even after asking questions or reviewing material, and 1 (4.8%) said most students are underchallenged, with several combined-response categories at roughly 9.5% each. The staff survey identified main themes needing to be addressed within the current math progression model: too much content in Honors Algebra 1 (combined with Math 8) at 7 respondents (33.3%), difficulty with differentiation regarding pacing, learning gaps, and student supports at 5 (23.8%), underchallenged students at 5 (23.8%), and a fear of lower outcomes for Algebra (with the count truncated in the extracted text).

Reflecting updated January 2026 MDE guidance emphasizing the least restrictive environment, students currently assigned program minutes in a special education resource room will instead be enrolled in general education courses with content-certified teachers while continuing to receive SDI as supplemental support. The letter is signed by Superintendent Richard Machesky, Ed.D., and lists Special Education leaders Sarah Smotherman, Jamie Evans, and Hillary Pulliam.

What it is
A letter from the Troy School District Special Education department to families, explaining a service-delivery change for the 2026-2027 school year.

Who it affects
- Secondary students in grades 6-12 who are diploma-bound and receive specially designed instruction (SDI) through their IEP.

Policy basis
- Updated Michigan Department of Education (MDE) guidance on delivering SDI in the least restrictive environment (LRE), so students learn alongside peers in general education with content-certified teachers while receiving individualized IEP support.
- MDE stresses SDI should supplement, not supplant, general education core content classes.

- Resource room program teachers continue providing SDI to meet IEP goals.

Ways support/SDI may be provided
- Push-in small-group or one-on-one support within the general education classroom.
- Pull-out small-group or one-on-one support outside the classroom.
- A scheduled hour dedicated to SDI and supports (Integrated Studies).
- Additional support during the day as determined by the IEP team.

https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose: A letter from the Troy School District Special Education department addressed to families, communicating a change in how services will be delivered for the 2026-2027 school year to secondary students in grades 6-12 who are diploma-bound and receive specially designed instruction (SDI) through their Individualized Education Program (IEP). The letter explains that the Michigan Department of Education (MDE) has updated its guidance to support students receiving SDI in the least restrictive environment (LRE), meaning students learn alongside their peers in general education classes taught by content-certified teachers while still receiving the individualized support they need to succeed through their IEP. It emphasizes MDE's position that SDI should be provided in addition to (as a supplement to) students' general education core content classes, not in replacement of (supplanting) those classes. As a practical result, diploma-bound students who currently have program minutes in a special education resource room will be enrolled in general education courses and receive SDI based on their IEP needs, with the specific SDI each student requires being an IEP team decision. Resource room program teachers will continue to provide SDI to meet IEP goals and objectives. The letter lists the ways support and SDI may be provided, including but not limited to: specially designed instruction and support in a small group or one-on-one within (push-in) the general education classroom; the same in a small group or one-on-one outside (pull-out) the general education classroom; a scheduled hour in a student's day dedicated to SDI and supports, described as Integrated Studies; and additional support during other parts of the school day as determined by the IEP team. Families are directed to the full January 2026 SDI guidance document from MDE and are encouraged to contact their school IEP team and building administrator with questions. The letterhead identifies the Special Education office at 4420 Livernois, Troy, Michigan 48098 (phone 248-823-5096) and names Sarah Smotherman, Director of Special Education, along with Supervisors of Special Education Jamie Evans and Hillary Pulliam. The letter is signed by Richard Machesky, Ed.D., Superintendent of Schools, and carries an Equal Opportunity/Affirmative Action Employer notice.

https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose: An informational overview and rankings list titled Section 35m Tier 1 Early Literacy Materials and Series (PK-5), part of the Troy School District's April 28, 2026 literacy pilot packet. It explains that Section 35m of the FY 2025 state School Aid Act provides $87 million to the Michigan Department of Education (MDE) to create a Committee for Literacy Achievement (CLA) and to allocate funding based on a rankings list of literacy tools and strategies recommended by the CLA, with the goal of increasing student academic outcomes in literacy. The CLA critically evaluated literacy tools and strategies across three categories - (1) literacy series and materials, (2) professional development, and (3) tools and services - all submitted through a Request for Submissions process, to make recommendations for grade-tier rankings. These evaluations produced three rankings lists: Tier 1 Early Literacy Curriculum Materials and Series, Early Literacy Interventions, and Professional Development, and the rankings serve as the basis for how funding is allocated to districts and intermediate districts. Districts apply for funding for one literacy item from one of the ranking lists. The Tier 1 Early Literacy Materials and Series were evaluated using The Reading League Curriculum Evaluation Guidelines, the EdReports 2.0 Review Criteria, and the ESSA Tiers of Evidence, and each entry links to a consensus scoring document. The Tier 1 rankings list, in order, is: (1) Amplify CKLA, 3rd Edition (2025); (2) Really Great Reading: Countdown (2023), Blast Foundations (2023), and HD Word (2023); (3) 95 Phonics Core Program, First Edition; (4) IMSE Orton-Gillingham Plus (OG+), 2025; (5) Imagine Learning EL Education Edition 1 (2019); (5) Wit & Wisdom (K-5 Core ELA program) and Geodes (K-3 Decodable Texts); (6) HMH Into Reading, 2025; (6) Story Champs 2.0 (2018); (7) UFLI Foundations, 1st Edition; (7) Magnetic Reading Foundations, 2023; and (8) Collaborative Literacy, 3rd Edition. The list includes tied rankings at positions 5, 6, and 7. Notably, Collaborative Literacy, 3rd Edition - the program the district's own K-5 reviewers overwhelmingly preferred in the concurrent pilot - appears at the bottom of the state's Tier 1 list at rank 8, while Amplify CKLA holds the top state ranking.

https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
A board consideration and accompanying resolution, listed under agenda item 10 ("OTHER"), subsection A, concerning the 2026 Oakland Schools Intermediate School District (ISD) Board of Education Biennial Election. One six-year term seat is open on the Oakland Schools board, and the document notes that a single candidate, Gary Hauff, has filed for it.

The document explains the ISD election mechanism: Oakland Schools board members are elected not by the general public but by an electoral body composed of one person designated by the board of each constituent school district. Under the Revised School Code, each constituent district's board must adopt a resolution that (1) designates a person to vote on the district's behalf, (2) directs that designee as to which candidate(s) the local board supports, and (3) directs the designee to vote for that individual at least on the first ballot taken by the electoral body. Designated electors must cast their ballots in person, and no absentee ballots are accepted. The election is scheduled for Monday, June 1, 2026, between 5:30 and 7:30 PM at the Oakland Schools Conference Center, 2111 Pontiac Lake Road, in Waterford.

The Resolution of the Troy Board of Education recites that Mich. Comp. Laws Sec. 380.614 requires a constituent board to designate its representative and identify the supported ISD candidate by a resolution adopted not earlier than 21 days before the election, that the statute prescribes consideration of the resolution at not less than one public meeting before adoption, and that the Board previously considered the resolution at an open meeting conducted under the Open Meetings Act on May 19, 2026.

The operative resolution provides that: the Board designates Kendra Montante as its representative, and a member of the Troy School District administration team as its alternate representative, to serve on the 2026 electoral body responsible for electing members to the Oakland Schools ISD Board of Education; the Board supports candidate Gary Hauff for the one open position for a term of six years ending June 30, 2032; and the Board directs its representative Kendra Montante to vote for Gary Hauff at least on the first ballot taken at the June 1, 2026 election.

The document includes blank "Yes" and "No" tally lines and the notation "Motion declared adopted," followed by a signature block for the Secretary of the Board of Education and a certification attesting that the foregoing is a true and complete copy of the resolution adopted by the Board. The certification's district-name, meeting-type, and date fields are left blank to be completed.

https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
Consideration Item 5.J. on the May 19, 2026 regular meeting consent agenda: a resolution directing the Troy School District to hold a public hearing on its proposed 2026-2027 school year budget. The recommended action is acceptance of the resolution.

The preamble recites Michigan law providing that every local unit of government, including a school district, must hold a public hearing on its proposed budget, with notice at least six days before the hearing; that the notice must state the time and place of the hearing and where a copy of the proposed budget is available for public inspection; and that the notice must include, in 11-point bold face type, the statement: "THE PROPERTY TAX MILLAGE RATE PROPOSED TO BE LEVIED TO SUPPORT THE PROPOSED BUDGET WILL BE A SUBJECT OF THIS HEARING." It states the hearing will be held at the Troy School District Services Building, 4420 Livernois Road, Troy 48098, beginning at 7:00 p.m. on Tuesday, June 16, 2026, and that copies of the proposed budget will be available for public inspection at the Administration Building, 4400 Livernois, Troy, Michigan 48098, from 8:00 a.m. until 4:30 p.m., Wednesday, June 10, 2026 through Tuesday, June 16 (the exhibit prints the closing year as 2025, an apparent typographical error).
